segments.text: Hey Marcus. How's it going? You look like you've been in the query planner for three days straight.
Ha, is it that obvious? Yeah, I'm good. Tired, but good. The funnel stuff finally clicked on Tuesday.
I saw. Two point eight seconds down to under a second. That's great work. I shared it in the leadership channel.
Oh, thanks. I didn't know that.
Yeah, Dana replied with three fire emojis, which for Dana is basically a standing ovation.
Ha, I'll take it.
So I have a couple of things I want to cover. Some feedback, and I want to talk about the staff engineer conversation we started last month. But first, anything on your mind? This is your time.
Yeah, actually, a couple of things. One is small. The on call rotation. I've been on it every third week for about eight months now and it's starting to wear on me a bit.
Okay. Tell me more. Is it the frequency or the pages themselves?
Mostly the pages. Like, I got woken up four times last rotation, and three of them were the same flaky disk alert on the old ingestion box. Nobody owns it, so it just keeps firing.
Ugh, yeah. That's not okay. That's a broken alert, not an on call problem.
Right. And I don't want to complain, but--

You're not complaining, this is exactly the kind of thing I want to hear. Two things. Nina joins the rotation next week, so you go from every third week to every fourth. And I'll ask Kevin to either fix or delete that disk alert by end of next week.
That would help a lot. Honestly just the disk alert would be most of it.
Okay, I'm writing that down. Kevin, disk alert, by end of next week. What's the second thing?
The second thing is bigger. It's about the AI Insights project. I keep hearing it's going to be the big Q4 bet, and I'm a bit worried about how it's being scoped.
Okay. Worried how?

So from what I've seen in the doc, the plan is to run an LLM over every customer's event stream every night and generate insights. But nobody's done the math on cost. For Globex alone that's something like four hundred million events a month.
Yeah. That's a fair concern. I've heard the same thing from Arjun.
And I think there's a smarter version where you precompute anomalies with plain statistics, and only send the interesting slices to the model. Like, ninety nine percent cheaper.
Have you written that down anywhere?
Not really. Just in my head and a couple of Slack threads.
Okay, so that's actually a nice segue into the feedback I wanted to give you. Can I share it now?
Yeah, go for it.

So the positive first, and I mean this. Your technical judgment is excellent. The funnel work, the way you debugged the rebalancing issue in July, people trust your calls. When Marcus says something is a bad idea, people listen.
Thanks. That's nice to hear.

The growth area is that a lot of that judgment stays in Slack threads and hallway conversations. Like what you just told me about AI Insights. That's a really important idea, and right now it lives in your head. If it's not written down, it doesn't influence the roadmap.
Yeah. That's, yeah. That's fair. I kind of hate writing docs. It feels slow.

I know. And I'm not asking for a forty page design doc. But at the staff level, the job is less about writing the best code and more about making sure the org makes the right technical decisions. And that happens in writing.
Okay. So for the AI Insights thing, what would you want to see?

A two page doc. What's the proposed approach, what's your approach, rough cost comparison, and the risks. If you can get that to me by tomorrow, Wednesday, I'll make sure it's pre-read for Q4 planning on Thursday.
Wednesday is tight, but doable. Can Hannah review it? She knows the model cost side way better than I do.
Yes, great idea. Loop her in. And honestly, that's another staff behavior, pulling in the right people.
Ha, look at me, being staff already.
Ha, one doc at a time. Okay, so that leads into the career conversation. Last month you said you wanted to go for staff engineer in the next cycle. Is that still true?
Yeah, definitely. I've been thinking about it a lot. I think I want it, but I also want to make sure I'm not just chasing a title.
That's a good instinct. What do you think it would mean for your day to day?
I guess less feature work, more cross team stuff. Setting technical direction. Maybe mentoring Nina and Aman more formally.
Yeah, that's about right. And for what it's worth, you already mentor Aman informally. He told me your code reviews are the most useful ones he gets.
Oh really? I always feel like I'm being too picky.
He said picky but kind. Which is the best combination.
Okay, I'll put that on my tombstone. Picky but kind.

Ha. So here's how I'd frame the gap. Our staff rubric has four areas: technical depth, scope of impact, written communication, and developing others. You're clearly at staff level on technical depth. Developing others, you're close. Scope and writing are where I need to see more evidence.
Okay. What does evidence look like for scope?

Owning something that spans more than one team. For example, the query engine migration. If you led that, deleting the old engine, coordinating with platform and the frontend team, that's a staff sized project.
Oh, I would love to kill the old query engine. I've been wanting to do that for a year.
I know, you mention it about once a week.
Ha, guilty.

So here's what I'm proposing. You write the AI Insights cost doc by Wednesday. Then, assuming it gets prioritized at planning, you lead the query engine migration in Q4, as the technical lead, including writing the design doc and running the weekly sync.
Okay. And the promo timeline?

Promo packets are due in mid January. If the migration is on track and you've got two or three solid docs under your belt by then, I'd feel really good about putting you up. I can't promise the committee outcome, but I'd advocate hard.
That's fair. I appreciate you being clear about it.
Can I ask something about the migration? If I'm leading it, who's actually doing the work? Because if it's just me, it's three weeks minimum, and I'd also be doing the cohorts rewrite.
Good question. I was thinking you plus Aman, with Nina for the frontend switchover at the end. And the cohorts rewrite would move to Aman after the webhook work, so you're not doing both.
Okay, that's much more realistic. Aman's ready for it, honestly. He's been asking for something meatier.
See, that's a staff sentence. You're thinking about Aman's growth, not just the project.
Ha, stop, you're going to make me self conscious about every sentence now.
Ha, sorry. But one thing to watch. Leading means you'll write less code. Some people really struggle with that. How do you feel about it?
Honestly, a bit nervous. Writing code is how I know I had a productive day. If I spend a day in meetings and docs, it feels like I did nothing.

That's super normal. One trick that helped me, write down at the end of each day what decisions got unblocked because of you. It's a different scoreboard. Try it for two weeks and tell me how it feels.
Okay, I'll try it. Decision journal. Very fancy.
One more piece of feedback, a smaller one. In the architecture review two weeks ago, when Tom pushed back on the caching approach, you kind of went quiet and then did it your way anyway.
Yeah. I noticed that too, after. I didn't really want to argue with the Head of Product in front of everyone.

I get it. But it ended up confusing people, because Tom thought we'd agreed to his approach. It's totally okay to disagree in the room. Tom actually likes it. He respects people who push back with data.
Okay. So next time, say it in the room. Or follow up in writing if it's not the right moment.
Exactly. Disagree and then commit, or disagree and then write it down. Either is fine. The quiet version isn't.
Got it. That's useful. Honestly I didn't realize it had that effect.
That's why I'm telling you. It's not a big deal, it was a one off. Anything you want from me? Feedback goes both ways.
Hmm. Maybe one thing. Sometimes priorities change mid sprint and I find out in standup instead of before. Like the sharing bug last week. It'd be nice to get a heads up.
That's fair. That one came from Siobhan late on Friday and I just dropped it in standup. I'll try to message the person directly before standup when something shifts. Call me out if I don't.
Will do. Politely.
Picky but kind.
Ha, exactly.

Okay, let me recap. I'll make sure Kevin fixes or deletes the flaky disk alert by end of next week, and Nina joins on call next week. You'll write the two page AI Insights cost doc with Hannah's review by Wednesday. If prioritized, you'll lead the query engine migration in Q4. And we'll check in on the promo packet in early December.
Sounds good. And you'll ping me before standup when priorities shift.
Yes. Deal. Thanks Marcus. Go get some sleep.
Ha, after one more query. Thanks Priya.

summaries.markdown:
# Priya / Marcus 1:1 — 1:1 summary

## Updates & wins
- Marcus cut funnel P95 from 2.8s to under a second; Priya shared it in the leadership channel.
- Aman says Marcus's code reviews are the most useful he gets: 'picky but kind'.

## Challenges
- On-call every third week for eight months; woken four times last rotation, three by the same flaky disk alert.
- Concern that AI Insights is scoped to run an LLM nightly over every event stream, which is ~400M events a month for Globex alone.
- Priority changes mid-sprint reach Marcus in standup rather than beforehand.

## Feedback
- Strength: excellent technical judgment that people trust.
- Growth area: judgment stays in Slack and hallways; if it isn't written down it doesn't shape the roadmap.
- In the architecture review Marcus went quiet on Tom's caching pushback and then did it his way; disagree in the room or in writing.
- For Priya: give a direct heads-up before standup when priorities shift.

## Career & growth
- Marcus wants staff engineer in the next cycle; he is at staff level on technical depth and close on developing others.
- Scope evidence: lead the query engine migration with Aman, and Nina on the frontend switchover.
- Promo packets due mid-January; Priya will advocate if the migration is on track with two or three solid docs.
- Keep a decision journal for two weeks to adjust to less coding.

## Next steps
- Kevin fixes or deletes the disk alert by end of next week; Nina joins on-call next week.
- Marcus writes a two-page AI Insights cost doc with Hannah's review by Wednesday, as a pre-read for Q4 planning.
- Promo packet check-in in early December.
